planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mrs. Moon is one of the oldest and most reliable pulmonaria cultivars, tolerating a wider range of conditions, including brief dry spells, better than many newer selections.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Mrs. Moon is a classic, long-cultivated pulmonaria selection bearing broad, softly hairy, dark green leaves heavily spotted with silvery-white blotches, forming an attractive textured groundcover that lasts well into fall. In early spring, clusters of funnel-shaped flowers open pink and mature to blue on the same stem, a color-changing display that gives lungwort its old-fashioned charm and provides an early nectar source for emerging bees. It is one of the toughest and most widely available pulmonaria cultivars, tolerating drier shade and a wider range of garden conditions than many newer, more finicky selections, making it a dependable choice for a woodland border or beneath deciduous shrubs. Cut back tattered summer foliage to encourage a fresh flush of clean leaves.

common_name: Ozark Premier Plum (Large Red Japanese-Type Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Ozark Premier requires roughly 800 chill hours and, although partially self-fruitful, produces a heavier crop with a compatible Japanese plum pollinator such as Methley or Morris planted nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart along the branch to encourage larger size and prevent limb breakage from a heavy crop. Developed in Arkansas and long a favorite in Southern orchards, Ozark Premier is a vigorous Japanese-type plum producing very large, round, red-skinned fruit with firm, juicy, amber-yellow flesh and a rich, sweet-tart flavor that holds up well for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. It ripens in mid to late summer and is partially self-fruitful, though yields improve significantly with a second compatible plum variety nearby for cross-pollination. The tree is vigorous and productive with moderate disease resistance for the region, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South home orchards where lower-chill plum selection is important. Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and fruit quality.

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or sulfur; Baldwin requires roughly 400–500 chill hours and is not self-fruitful, needing a cross-pollinating rabbiteye companion such as Tifblue, Climax, or Brightwell nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive conditions rabbiteye blueberries need. Baldwin is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening quite late in the season, extending the blueberry harvest well past earlier cultivars, with small to medium, firm, dark blue berries that hold their shape and flavor well, making them useful for fresh eating, freezing, and machine harvest alike. The plant is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the acidic, sandy soils typical of the Gulf South, requiring a second compatible rabbiteye variety nearby for good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or sulfur; Tara requires roughly 350–450 chill hours and is not self-fruitful, needing a cross-pollinating rabbiteye companion nearby for reliable fruit set.

directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to retain the consistent soil moisture rabbiteye blueberries need for good fruit size. Tara is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release prized for its early ripening and consistently light, sky-blue berries with excellent flavor and a small, dry picking scar that resists splitting and leaking, an important trait for fresh-market and pick-your-own plantings. The bush is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the sandy, acidic soils of the Gulf South, extending the early end of the rabbiteye blueberry season when planted alongside later-ripening cultivars. Plant with a second compatible rabbiteye variety for good cross-pollination, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive.
